title: Plans
description: Talk about tomorrow, the weekend and your dreams.

words.notes: nja + ku- verb: nja kugenda, I will go.
The ku- form after nja: nja kugenda.

sentences.base: Tomorrow I will go to Masaka.
altBase: I will go to Masaka tomorrow.
I am going to eat matooke.
We are going to study together.

sentences.base: At the weekend I will visit grandparent.
altBase: At the weekend I will visit grandma.
On the weekend I will visit grandpa.
This weekend I will visit my grandparent.
At the weekend I’ll visit grandma.

sentences.target: Wiiki ejja tujja kugenda e Jinja.
sentences.base: Next week we will go to Jinja.
altBase: We will go to Jinja next week.
Next week we’re going to Jinja.

sentences.base: Next year I will study science.
altBase: I will study science next year.

sentences.base: One day I will go to Buganda.
altBase: Someday I will go to Buganda.
One day I’ll go to Buganda.

sentences.base: One day I will speak Luganda well.
altBase: Someday I will speak Luganda well.
One day I’ll speak Luganda well.

sentences.base: I hope to see the Kabaka.
altBase: I hope to see the king.

sentences.base: What are you planning for the weekend?
altBase: What are your plans for the weekend?
What are you planning at the weekend?

dialogues.speaker: ssali
dialogues.base: What are you planning for the weekend?

guidebook.intro: Talking about the future lets you make plans, promises and dreams. Luganda has a near future and a far one.

phrases.base: Tomorrow I will go to Masaka.
What are you planning for the weekend?
At the weekend I will visit grandparent.
One day I will speak Luganda well.
I hope to see the Kabaka.

tips.title: Soon: ja + ku-
body: The near future uses **-jja** (come) with the **ku-** form, a bit like English “going to”: **nja kugenda** (I will go), **ojja kugenda**, **ajja kugenda**, **tujja kugenda**, **bajja kugenda**.
The **o-** of the infinitive drops: **okulya** becomes **kulya** after **nja**.

tips.title: Someday: li-
body: For the distant or less certain future, add **-li-**: **ndigenda** (I will go, someday), **ndyogera** (I will speak). Pair it with **olunaku lumu** (one day).

culture.title: Plans and “Katonda bw’anaayagala”
body: Many Ugandans add **Katonda bw’anaayagala** (God willing) when talking about the future, much like “inshallah”. You’ll hear it at the end of plans of every size.

stories.title: Weekend plans
stories.summary: Ssali and Nakato talk about last weekend and the next one.

line.speaker: ssali
line.base: Nakato! What did you do last weekend?

line.speaker: nakato
line.base: I went to Masaka to visit my mother.

steps.question: Where did Nakato go last weekend?

line.speaker: nakato
line.base: I don’t know. What are you planning?

line.speaker: ssali
line.target: Nja kugenda ku nnyanja e Entebbe. Ojja?
line.base: I’m going to the lake in Entebbe. Are you coming?

line.speaker: nakato
line.base: Yes! But I don’t have much money.

line.speaker: ssali
line.target: Totya. Tujja kugenda mu mmotoka yange.
line.base: Don’t worry. We’ll go in my car.

steps.question: How does Ssali say “We will go”?

line.speaker: nakato
line.base: Thank you very much! See you on Saturday.
